subject: chemistry
title: Reading the Periodic Table
welcome_lead: A grid of all known elements, arranged by a clever code. Crack it.
meta_desc: Learn how the periodic table is organised in this KS3 chemistry adventure.
final_note: You can now navigate the periodic table with confidence.

concepts.def: Chart of all elements, organised by atomic number.
Number of protons in an atom; identifies the element.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Elements are arranged in order of their atomic number. Hydrogen is #1, helium is #2, lithium is #3, and so on.

Atomic number = number of protons.

The vertical columns are called groups. Elements in the same group have similar properties.

The horizontal rows are called periods.

Metals are on the LEFT and middle (most of the table).
Non-metals are on the RIGHT.
A zig-zag staircase line divides them.

mcqs.q: When water boils, what is broken?
options: Intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds) between water molecules are broken — the O-H covalent bonds stay intact.
Entropy measures how much energy a system contains in total.
The covalent bonds between hydrogen and oxygen atoms are broken when water boils.
Water molecules split into hydrogen and oxygen gas when they boil.

mcqs.q: How does a fuel cell differ from a conventional battery?
options: Fuel cells burn fuel to generate heat which is then converted to electricity.
Water molecules split into hydrogen and oxygen gas when they boil.
Fuel cells and batteries are identical — both just store electrical energy.
A fuel cell continuously consumes externally supplied fuel (e.g. hydrogen) and oxidant; a battery has a fixed amount of reactants that get used up.

mcqs.q: What does an increase in entropy of a system correspond to?
options: Entropy is just a measure of how messy a system looks visually.
An increase in the number of ways energy and particles can be arranged — typically a more dispersed/'disordered' state.
Entropy measures how much energy a system contains in total.
Water molecules split into hydrogen and oxygen gas when they boil.
